source.title: Scaling Laws for Looped Mixture of Experts
source.authors: Yan-Bei Chen; Anirudh Goyal; Raghuraman Krishnamoorthi

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study fits loss-scaling laws and evaluates held-out loss predictions, using a related scaling-sweep and fitting approach on looped dense and looped MoE models. Its added recurrence and sparsity axes and bounded recurrence mapping make this an extension of the original setup.
record.gate_note: The paper reports held-out loss RMSEs for alternative recurrence mappings, fitted scaling-law coefficients, and downstream benchmark scores. It also reports expert-path diversity and figures on scaling and IsoFLOP trends; routing diversity is not itself a measure of the claim's loss scaling, and plotted downstream values not given numerically in the text are not recorded as numeric rows.
record.test_reason: The study fits parametric loss laws over active parameters, tokens, expert count and recurrence for looped dense and MoE transformers trained from scratch, and scores held-out loss prediction. That bears on V1, V2 and V7 in a new architecture setting rather than the originals' plain dense setup, so T3 fits better than T1. Downstream scaling with training compute (Figure 7) bears qualitatively on V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that a bounded, sparsity-conditional recurrence mapping in a unified law over N, D, R and E predicts held-out loss better than linear or power-law mappings, and that it recovers the dense and MoE laws as special cases. They add that it guides compute- and memory-constrained design, that sparsity gives about 3x active-parameter efficiency and recurrence about 2x total-parameter efficiency on reasoning, and that a law-derived looped MoE matches a 2x larger MoE on reasoning at trillion-token scale.
record.recipe_differences: Uses loss-scaling sweeps and held-out prediction comparisons like the original scaling-law work, but extends the fitted form with recurrence, MoE expert expansion, and a bounded effective-parameter mapping. The paper also uses a staged fit and log-Huber refinement.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted recurrence mapping matters: linear, power-law, bounded, and sparsity-conditional bounded alternatives give different held-out RMSEs. The paper does not vary fitting choices to assess their sensitivity.

fits_no_version.finding: Test-time recurrence on one LoopMoE checkpoint raises the 14-benchmark mean from 36.6 to 46.9 over R=1–5, with diminishing returns.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream performance of looped models scales with test-time recurrence, saturating within a few passes.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched training compute, the law-selected LoopMoE (R*=5, 0.3B active) roughly matches a 2x larger MoE on BBH/GSM8K but trails it overall (46.9 vs 50.2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Recurrence substitutes for parameters on reasoning tasks but not on knowledge-heavy tasks.

record.problems: The loss scaling and prediction tests use a specific looped architecture setup and a limited sweep; the reported held-out recurrence test is R=16 after fitting on R≤8, not an orders-of-magnitude scale extrapolation. The paper reports bootstrap intervals for selected fitted coefficients, but not uncertainty intervals for the held-out RMSEs. Downstream scores are reported without uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 reports scores for additional individual benchmarks beyond BBH and GSM8K; these per-task rows are omitted in favor of the two reasoning tasks and 14-benchmark mean, which are the comparisons emphasized in the text. Figure 7 also shows downstream scaling curves, but most plotted values are not stated numerically in the text.

untested.parts: Power-law behaviour over several orders of magnitude. N spans 0.3–1.0B and D spans 100–500B. No compute-only law is fitted.
Prediction of runs orders of magnitude larger. Held-out slices are R=16, E=16, the top N, and D in (400,500]B. The 1.5e22-FLOP trillion-token runs report no observed-vs-predicted loss.
Not tested. Optimal N/D splits and R* come from the fitted law and are not verified empirically. There is no Kaplan vs Hoffmann allocation comparison.
Not tested. The ladder varies depth and width together with size.
Not tested. All runs are text pretraining.
No quantitative mapping from loss or scale to downstream scores. Figure 7 values are plotted only.
Parameter-counting conventions, training schedule, data and optimiser choices are not varied. Only the recurrence functional form and the number of sparsity exponents are compared.

missing.what: Downstream Overall and Reasoning scores versus training FLOPs across model size, expert count and recurrence. The text says scores improve consistently with sparsity and recurrence at matched compute, but no values are stated.
Ablation with separate sparsity exponents θ1, θ2 gives the same RMSE of 0.0037, so the extra exponent adds nothing.
Empirical loss versus recurrence plateaus within R≤8, with dense models saturating earlier than MoE.
Bootstrap CIs on the joint optimum collapse to single configurations across 100 refits.

record.verdict_notes: Changes to the record's labels. Tranche T1 becomes T3, because the setting is a new architecture. V7 changes from 'challenges' to 'supports': poor extrapolation by the unbounded mappings shows that fit-form choice drives predictions, which is what V7 says. Competing-mapping rows move from V2 to V7. Table 2 rows are unlinked: they measure test-time recurrence on a single checkpoint, not pretraining scale. The V6 verdict and the V2 and V7 labels below rest on the text and figures. The sweep range is narrow, so V1 and V2 support is weak and confined to that range.

versions.untested_parts: Tests fitted loss scaling over model size and training tokens in looped dense and MoE settings; does not establish the original claim across the full range of ordinary dense language-model runs or several orders of magnitude.
Tests held-out recurrence, expert-count, model-size, and data slices, including recurrence R=16 after fitting on R≤8. Does not test predictions for runs orders of magnitude larger.

The paper optimizes recurrence and expert count under compute and memory constraints, but does not test stable power-law growth of loss-minimizing parameter and token counts with compute or compare the Kaplan and Hoffmann parameter/token allocation trends.
Does not compare depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Studies language-model pretraining, not other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Reports downstream benchmark performance across recurrence, sparsity, and compute settings, but does not fit or test a quantitative mapping from held-out pretraining loss to downstream performance.

Tests whether recurrence curves are better represented by bounded rather than unbounded linear or power-law mappings. Does not vary fitting procedures, parameter-count conventions, or training schedules to measure fit-choice sensitivity, nor test why published parameter/token exponents disagree.

relation.reason: Its own training sweeps, fitted loss laws and held-out comparisons directly examine scaling behavior and fitting choices.

tranche.reason: The study fits and evaluates loss-scaling laws in the new setting of jointly varied recurrence and MoE sparsity.

source_check.notes: Appendix C.3 reports more than 1,000 loss observations, not explicitly more than 1,000 distinct training runs. The trillion-token experiment validates downstream utility of law-guided design, without validating its loss forecasts.
